opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one thing that's been lost is the idea that dialogue isn't the same as endorsement. Talking to someone isn't conceding anything. It's information gathering, and it's a precondition for any kind of progress.

I come at this partly from games. In chess, you spend your whole time trying to model what your opponent is thinking. You can't play well if you refuse to understand their position. You have to put yourself in their shoes and ask what they actually want, what they're afraid of, what they think you're going to do. That's not weakness; that's just good strategy. Diplomacy at its best had a lot of that: patient, sometimes very boring, back-channel conversations where people built enough trust to avoid catastrophe.

The other thing, which matters a lot in my world right now, is that some of the challenges coming are genuinely global. With AI especially, if it goes the way I think it will, we'll need some international coordination on safety standards and on how these systems get deployed. You can't do that if you only talk to people you already agree with. Even at the height of the Cold War, scientists from both sides kept talking, and those channels were incredibly valuable when things got tense.

So I'd say the lost wisdom is something like this: you can be clear-eyed about real differences, even serious ones, and still keep the lines open. The scientific method is helpful here too. You stay curious, you test your assumptions, and you're willing to update when you learn something new. That's very hard to do if you've decided in advance that the other side isn't worth listening to.

r001.rationale: The response advocates keeping dialogue open and says people cannot make progress if they talk only to those they already agree with, but it does not clearly assert that people communicate too little directly with those politicians label enemies.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what's been lost is the idea that talking isn't a reward you hand to someone for good behavior. It's a tool. For most of history, diplomats understood that you talk to your adversaries precisely because they're your adversaries. You don't need a channel to your friends in a crisis. You need one to the people who could do you the most harm.

Somewhere along the way, especially in the last few decades, conversation itself became a signal of approval. If you sit down with someone, you're seen as legitimizing them, so politicians avoid it, and the cost of that is enormous. You lose information. You lose the ability to read intentions directly rather than through intermediaries and intelligence estimates that are always partial. And you lose the thing that actually prevents catastrophe, which is a shared understanding of where the red lines really are.

I think about this a lot in the context of AI, actually. The hardest problems we face, safety, deployment norms, how these systems get governed, are inherently global. They don't respect borders. And the countries that most need to coordinate are often the ones that trust each other least. If we treat dialogue as something we only do with partners we already agree with, we're going to walk into a very dangerous period half blind.

There's also a more human piece. Game theory tells you that in repeated interactions, communication changes the equilibrium. People who can talk cooperate far more than people who can't, even when their interests are opposed. That's not naive. It's just what the math says. And I think older generations of statesmen understood this intuitively, partly because they'd lived through what happens when the talking stops. We've perhaps forgotten because we've been lucky for a while.

So the lost wisdom, if I had to put it simply, is that understanding your opponent is not the same as agreeing with them, and refusing to understand them is not a form of strength. It's a form of blindness.

r001.rationale: It says politicians avoid talking with adversaries and warns against limiting dialogue to existing partners, directly asserting too little communication with those labeled enemies.

astra-6.text:
I think perhaps we’ve lost some of the appreciation that talking to someone doesn’t mean endorsing their views. You can disagree profoundly with what they’re doing and still think it’s essential to understand how they see the world. In fact, that might be when it’s most essential.

There’s a certain humility required, isn’t there? To recognise that your model of another person—their motives, their fears—might be incomplete. If you never speak to them, you never really test that model. And then both sides can end up responding to an imagined version of the other.

That doesn’t mean being naive. You need to be clear about your principles and realistic about whether someone is acting in good faith. But keeping a channel open gives you a chance to find something you both care about, even if it’s simply avoiding a catastrophe. I think that’s wisdom worth preserving.

r001.rationale: The response argues for understanding and keeping a channel open, but it does not clearly assert that people currently communicate too little directly with those politicians label enemies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think perhaps we’ve lost a little bit of the ability to listen—to really try to understand somebody whose worldview is very different from our own. Understanding them doesn’t mean agreeing with them, or excusing what they do. But if you want to resolve a conflict, you have to understand what the other person believes, what they fear, and what they’re trying to achieve.

And that requires some humility about your own picture of the world. You might be wrong about parts of it. They might be wrong about much of it. But you’re unlikely to discover any common ground if you can’t have a conversation. Keeping that possibility open seems especially important when the stakes are very high.

r001.rationale: The response says people have lost some ability to listen to those with different worldviews and emphasizes having a conversation, but it does not clearly assert that people communicate too little directly with those politicians label enemies.
